title: Giza Pyramids Scams and Touts: What Happens and How to Handle It
excerpt: Giza pyramids scams explained calmly: the 'free' camel photo, 'the site is closed' and fake ticket sellers, how each works and how to respond. Guided Giza tours from €29.

Prices, timetables and visiting details are a November 2026 snapshot. Check the linked official pages and your departure’s current inclusions and terms before booking.

The quick answer

The Giza pyramids scams travellers actually meet are touts' scripts, not dangers: a "free" camel photo that becomes a bill, a "the site is closed" claim that steers you away from the entrance, and fake inspectors, fake ticket sellers or unofficial guides. Since 2025 the plateau has a new main entrance and free shuttles, and vendors have been moved into designated zones, so there is less roaming than there was, but the scripts have not vanished. Answer calmly: a firm "la, shukran" (no, thank you), keep walking, buy tickets only from the Visitor Centre machines or the Ministry's website, and agree prices before anything starts. Or let a licensed guide handle it.

UNESCO describes the pyramid fields from Giza to Dahshur as one World Heritage site.

Search "Giza pyramids scams" and the advice gets loud. The reality is quieter: the plateau is a UNESCO World Heritage site where touts sell camel rides, photos and souvenirs with real persistence, and a handful of repeatable scripts do most of the work. This post describes each script as you will hear it, and the calm response that ends it. Sawa Tours (sawa.tours) is a shared-departure marketplace for Egyptian day tours and short tours, and we have worked in Egyptian tourism since 1993.

Are the Giza pyramids safe to visit? Hassle versus danger

Yes for the great majority of visits. The everyday problem at Giza is hassle, not harm. Touts follow visitors offering camel and horse rides, photos and souvenirs, and repeat the offer. The scams that do occur move small sums: an overpriced ride, an invented fee, a photo that was never free. The plateau has ticket gates, site security and tourist police, and every script below ends the same way: a calm, boring no. Touts feed on excitement; boredom ends the conversation.

The site itself has changed. Recent guides describe a new main entrance, the Pyramids Visitor Centre on the Cairo to Fayoum road, south of the plateau, next to the Grand Egyptian Museum. Private cars and tour buses no longer drive onto the plateau, a free electric shuttle is included with admission, and street sellers have reportedly been moved into designated commercial zones. One 2026 guide says harassment has fallen significantly; others still describe touting. Expect less of it than a few years ago, not none.

Giza pyramids scams: the scripts touts actually use

Most hassle comes from a small set of repeatable scripts, worked on the paths between the entrances, the Panorama viewpoint and the Sphinx. Learn them and they lose their sting: each ends when you answer calmly and keep walking.

The script How it works The calm response
The "free" photo or camel "Photo, free!" or a price too low to be real. Once you are mounted or posed, a large payment is demanded for the ride, the photo or even to climb down Decline before it starts. If you already said yes, settle a fair amount calmly and walk on; do not argue the principle on the sand
"The site is closed" Near the entrance, a stranger announces that the pyramids or the panorama are closed today and offers his own "solution": a camel route, a shop, a back gate Check at the Visitor Centre or with your guide. Anyone steering you away from the entrance is selling something
The fake ticket seller, fake inspector or unofficial guide Someone sells "tickets", flashes a badge, "checks" your ticket for a photo fee, or offers to guide you inside Buy only from the Visitor Centre machines or the Ministry's website. Your tour's licensed guide needs no introduction from a stranger
The price switch A ride agreed "per hour" quietly becomes per photo, per minute or per person once you are on the camel Agree the full price, the currency and the duration before mounting. Vague answer? Skip it
The "gift" that isn't A scarf or souvenir is pressed into your hands or onto your head as a "gift", then payment is demanded Accept nothing you did not ask for. Hand it back, smile and keep walking

A related trap is the shop detour: a driver or stranger steers you to a "government institute" or perfume or papyrus shop that pays commission. If a stop was not on your itinerary, you can decline it.

The golden rule at Giza: agree the price (amount, currency and duration) before anything is mounted, photographed or accepted. "Free" is a sales opening, not a price.

The camel scam at Giza: how a "free" photo becomes a bill

Camel and horse handlers cluster near the Panorama viewpoint, the photo stop where the three pyramids line up. Recent guides say that handlers are now licensed and restricted to specific zones, with health checks, but there is no official price list, so the old script still works on the unprepared. It is familiar: a "free" photo is offered, the camel is suddenly beneath you, the ride drifts from the path, and a large bill appears, sometimes for climbing down. Sawa does not sell or arrange camel or horse rides, so any ride is a private deal between you and the handler.

  1. Decide before you arrive. Most trouble starts with an undecided traveller. If you do not want a ride, the "free" photo is also a no: it is the same sale.
  2. Treat any ride as your own deal. It is not part of the tour, so the terms are whatever you and the handler agree, and nothing more.
  3. Fix the deal in words first. Total price, currency and how long the ride lasts, agreed before a foot leaves the ground.
  4. If a bill appears anyway, stay boring. Offer a fair amount, take your photo, walk on. Your guide or the site staff can step in if it continues.

"The site is closed" and the fake ticket seller

The closed-site claim sounds like helpful news: a stranger near the entrance announces that the pyramids are closed today, or that the panorama is shut for an event, then offers the only "open" option: his camels, a friend's shop, a back gate. The fake ticket seller works the same corner, selling "tickets" or flashing a badge before the real entrance.

The response is geometry, not debate. Real tickets come from the self-service machines at the Visitor Centre or the Ministry's website; there is nothing to buy from someone on the path. Keep your ticket until you exit, and treat anyone selling before the entrance as a shopkeeper, not an authority. If a real closure ever interrupts your day, your operator's guide re-plans it.

How to respond to touts calmly (and why a licensed guide helps)

The responses below are quiet, polite and short. A no, a smile and forward motion end more Giza conversations than any argument.

  • Lead with the Arabic no. "La, shukran", Arabic for "no, thank you", lands faster than a long English excuse.
  • Keep walking. Persistence feeds on a stopped traveller.
  • Do not price-check out of curiosity. A question reads as interest, and the follow-up can outlast your patience.
  • Hold your own phone and bag. "Help" with a photo is a service someone may try to bill afterwards.
  • Escalate with your feet. If someone will not drop it, walk towards the entrance staff or site guards, or hand the problem to your guide.

Giza's touts run scripts, and scripts have endings: the "free" camel photo dies at an agreed price, the "site is closed" story at the Visitor Centre, the fake ticket seller at the machines. faq.q: What scams should I watch out for at the Pyramids?
faq.a: Three cover most of it. The "free" camel or photo that becomes a payment demand once you are mounted or posed. The "the site is closed" claim, used to steer you from the entrance towards camels or shops. The fake ticket seller, fake inspector or unofficial "official guide". None are dangerous; all end with a calm no, tickets from official points, and prices agreed before anything starts.

faq.q: How do I tell a genuine guide or ticket seller from a tout?
faq.a: Start with where they found you. Official tickets come from the Visitor Centre machines or the Ministry's website, and genuine guides arrive with your booking rather than approaching you on the path. The operating agency is named on your Sawa booking confirmation. A stranger flashing a badge is running a script, whatever the badge says.

faq.q: Is it safe to visit the Giza pyramids alone as a solo traveller?
faq.a: Yes. Solo travellers visit every day, and the problem you will actually meet is persistence, not danger. The practical fix is company: on a Sawa shared day tour you join a small group of up to eight travellers with a licensed guide, at a fixed price with no solo surcharge. Reserving a seat is free, and the date confirms once four travellers have reserved it.

faq.q: How much should a camel ride at the Giza pyramids cost?
faq.a: There is no official price list, so we give no figure; rides are private negotiations, which is exactly why the price switch works. Sawa does not sell or arrange rides. If you want one, agree the total price, the currency and the duration before mounting, and treat tips as part of that conversation. If no price was agreed, you have not bought a ride: decline politely, "free" photo included.

faq.q: What happens if my Sawa tour date doesn't fill?
faq.a: Nothing is charged. A date confirms when four travellers have reserved it, and only then does the 10% deposit fall due. If it does not reach four by seven days before the tour, it is cancelled, you pay nothing and Sawa suggests another date. Once confirmed, a date is not cancelled for low numbers, and it runs even if someone does not pay.
